title: Prenatal Development
points: Prenatal development starts at conception, when one sperm fertilizes one egg to form a zygote.
The germinal stage covers the first 2 weeks.
The embryonic stage runs from week 3 to week 8.
The fetal stage runs from week 9 until birth.
The age of viability — when a fetus could survive outside the womb — is around 24 to 26 weeks.

title: Newborn Reflexes and Abilities
points: The rooting reflex helps newborns find food — stroking the cheek makes the baby turn toward the touch.
The palmar grasp reflex makes babies grip anything touching their palm.
The stepping reflex looks like the baby is trying to walk.
Newborns are not helpless.
Babies are born preferring faces.

title: Infant Sensory Development
points: Newborn vision is blurry and color-blind at first, but improves fast.
Scientists study infant senses with the preferential looking method — babies stare longer at what interests them.
Hearing develops before birth — newborns recognize their mother's voice and prefer lullabies heard in the womb.
Taste and smell work from birth.
Touch is the most developed sense at birth and stays vital.

title: Piaget: Sensorimotor Stage
points: The sensorimotor stage (birth to 2 years) is when babies learn through senses and movement.
In the secondary circular reactions substage (4 to 8 months), babies repeat actions that affect the world — shaking, banging,...
Coordination of secondary schemes (8 to 12 months) brings intentional problem-solving.
Object permanence — knowing things exist even when unseen — develops around 8 to 12 months.
The A-not-B error shows object permanence is still fragile.

title: Piaget: Preoperational Stage
points: The preoperational stage (ages 2 to 7) brings symbolic thinking — language, pretend play, and drawings explode.
Egocentrism is not selfishness — the child genuinely cannot imagine a different perspective.
Conservation is understanding that amount stays the same despite shape changes.
Children overextend words and show animism — believing lifeless things are alive (the moon follows me).
Artificialism is the belief that natural things are made by people — the clouds are made by someone pouring water.

title: Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory
points: Vygotsky said learning is social first — children learn through interaction with others, then internalize it.
The Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) is the gap between what a child can do alone and what she can do with help.
Scaffolding means giving temporary support — hints, models, reminders — and removing it as the child improves.
The More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) is anyone who knows more — teacher, parent, or peer.
Private speech — children talking to themselves during tasks — is not a bad habit.

title: Language Development Milestones
points: Cooing (around 2 months) is the first speech-like sound — vowel-like noises made during happy moments.
Babbling (around 6 months) adds consonants.
First words appear around 12 months, often as holophrases — one word carrying a whole sentence's meaning.
Early word meanings are messy.
Telegraphic speech (around 2 years) strings two words together, dropping extras like a telegram: want cookie.

title: Temperament in Infancy
points: Temperament is a baby's built-in style of reacting to the world — activity level, mood, and adaptability.
Thomas and Chess studied babies and found three types.
Difficult children (about 10%) are intense, irregular, and slow to adapt.
Slow-to-warm-up children (about 15%) are shy and cautious with new things but adapt gradually.
Goodness of fit is the key idea — outcomes depend on how well parenting matches the child's temperament.

title: Play and Development
points: Mildred Parten described play stages.
Parallel play (around age 3) means playing beside, not with, other children.
Associative play (around 4) brings real interaction — sharing, talking, borrowing toys — but no shared goal.
Pretend play peaks between ages 3 and 6 and builds crucial skills — language, creativity, emotion control, and understanding...
Games with rules (from age 6) teach fairness, turn-taking, and handling losing.

title: Theory of Mind
points: Theory of mind is understanding that others have thoughts, beliefs, and feelings different from your own.
The false-belief task is the classic test.
The Sally-Anne test asks where someone with outdated information will search.
Theory of mind powers kindness.
Autism involves theory-of-mind difficulties — reading faces, guessing intentions, and understanding jokes or sarcasm is hard.

title: Childhood Friendships
points: Early friendships are based on convenience and shared activities.
By middle childhood, friendship means intimacy — sharing secrets, helping with problems, and standing up for each other.
Peer status matters.
One good friendship protects against bullying, loneliness, and depression.
Friends influence each other strongly, for good and bad.

title: Parenting Styles (Baumrind)
points: Authoritative parents are warm but firm — high expectations plus high responsiveness.
Authoritarian parents are strict but cold — high demands, low warmth.
Permissive parents are warm but undemanding — few rules, little discipline.
Uninvolved (neglectful) parents are low on both warmth and control — the worst combination.
Baumrind studied American families, and culture shapes the details — but the core finding holds globally.

title: Puberty and the Adolescent Brain
points: Puberty starts with a growth spurt — girls around 10 to 11, boys around 12 to 13.
Puberty timing varies widely — anywhere from 8 to 14 is normal.
The adolescent brain is under construction.
Teens take more risks with peers watching — the brain's reward centers light up stronger for peer approval.
Synaptic pruning removes weak brain connections while myelination speeds up important ones.

title: Identity Formation (Marcia)
points: Erikson named adolescence the identity versus role confusion stage.
Identity diffusion: no exploration, no commitment.
Identity foreclosure: commitment without exploration.
Identity moratorium: active exploration without commitment yet.
Identity achievement: exploration followed by real commitment.

title: Peer Pressure in Adolescence
points: Peer pressure peaks around age 14.
Most peer pressure is unspoken — no one orders you, but you feel the pull.
Cliques are small, tight friendship groups; crowds are bigger reputation groups (athletes, nerds).
Peer influence is not all bad — friends boost school effort, kindness, and healthy habits as easily as risky ones.
Resistance skills work: having ready responses, suggesting alternatives, and keeping one sober friend nearby.

title: Risk Taking in Teens
points: Teen risk-taking is real — car crashes are the top killer of teens worldwide.
The dual systems model explains it: the socioemotional system (rewards, excitement) matures early in puberty, while the...
Surprising finding: teens often know the risks better than adults think.
Two modes of thinking: hot (emotional, rushed, with peers) versus cold (calm, alone, reflective).
Sensation seeking is normal and even useful — it drives exploration and independence.

title: Emerging Adulthood
points: Jeffrey Arnett named ages 18 to 25 emerging adulthood — a distinct stage in modern societies.
Five features define it: identity exploration (especially love and work), instability (moving, changing plans), self-focus...
This stage exists because life changed — longer education, later marriage, and tougher job markets delay adult roles.
The dark side: all this freedom brings the highest rates of mental health struggles.
The bright side: it is the freest period of life for self-discovery.

title: Transition to Parenthood
points: A baby's arrival is a major life transition — joy mixed with exhaustion.
The dip is well-documented: less time together, more conflict, divided attention.
Division of labor decides outcomes.
Postpartum depression affects about 1 in 7 mothers (and some fathers).
Social support is the top buffer — helpful family, friends, parent groups.

title: Midlife: Crisis or Myth?
points: The midlife crisis — a dramatic meltdown at 40 — is largely a myth.
Erikson called midlife's task generativity versus stagnation — contributing to the next generation through parenting,...
The sandwich generation cares for children and parents simultaneously.
Happiness dips in the 40s and 50s (the U-bend), then rises again.
Midlife often brings a mortality wake-up — health scares or losing a parent.

title: Successful Aging
points: Rowe and Kahn defined successful aging as three parts: avoiding disease and disability, staying mentally and physically...
Baltes' SOC model: Selection (choose fewer, meaningful goals), Optimization (practice what matters), Compensation (find new...
Age beliefs are powerful: positive views of aging add years to life and protect memory.
Lifestyle pillars: regular movement, Mediterranean-style eating, 7 to 8 hours of sleep, stress management, and never smoking.
Relationships are the top predictor — the Harvard happiness study found warm bonds keep people healthier into their 80s.
